messageText: This one's a catch-all server. Not every project is a year-long thing with a whole team behind it, some of them are a few months, one client, one very specific problem to solve.
So instead of giving each of those their own server, they each get a channel in here.
Pick a channel to read about one.

Vincent Di Fate is a sci-fi and aerospace illustrator, he's been painting book covers and NASA art for decades. He already had a portfolio site up for his artwork, and he wanted to start actually selling prints from it.
So the ask was a store. We went with Shopify for it, mainly because he needed the checkout, inventory and orders to just work without me building a whole backend for it.
Store's live here: https://shop.vincentdifate.com/collections/all
The catch with Shopify is that the theme layer is Liquid, which is server-rendered templating. You can't just drop a React component into it.

So I built the whole UI as Web Components with Lit instead. Custom elements are just HTML at the end of the day, so a Liquid template can render <vdf-shop-card> and the browser knows what to do with it. No framework needed on the theme side.
Every component got built in Storybook first, before it ever touched the store.
That was the whole workflow: build it in isolation, get the states right, then go integrate it. Way less painful than debugging styling inside a live Shopify theme.
Some of the components from the library:

On the build side: Vite bundles all the components into a single web-components.bundle.js, and there's a Make target that builds it and drops it plus the global CSS straight into the theme's assets folder. The theme.liquid just loads it with a defer tag.
make dev-serve-storybook for component work, make dev-serve-shopify to run the theme against a dev store. Two commands, that's the whole dev setup.

Started from Shopify's Dawn theme and forked it into a custom vincent-theme, overriding the sections I needed (product, collection grid, search, cart, header, footer) and leaving the rest of Dawn's plumbing alone.
Wrapped it up in December. The search results page reuses the same grid and filters as the collection page, cart got styled to match, and everything's responsive down to mobile.
Skill sheet for this one:
✅ Web Components  ✅ Lit  ✅ TypeScript  ✅ Storybook  ✅ Vite
✅ Shopify  ✅ Liquid  ✅ Shadow DOM  ✅ CSS Custom Properties
✅ Agile Methodologies  ✅ Project Management  ✅ Communication
Go poke at it: https://shop.vincentdifate.com/collections/all
Yonder Media Mobile is a mobile/media company out of New York. This one was a promo page, a single landing page that needed to be up for a couple of months and then go away.
Freelance gig, and it was basically all mine: the front-end, the CMS behind it, and the Docker setup it ran on. One page, but the ask was make it look expensive.
Above you can see the page itself and the Craft side as well.
Craft CMS was the pick, mostly because the whole point was that they could change the copy without calling me every time.

I set up two sections in Craft: mainContent for the blocks in the body, footerContent for the footer links. The Twig template just loops over the entries and renders whatever's there, so adding a block to the page was them clicking 'new entry', not me redeploying.
Front-end is hand-written Twig, CSS and vanilla JS. No framework, no build step. For a page this size that was the right call.

The motion is three things stacked: ScrollOut for the scroll-triggered reveals, Rellax for the parallax on the big vertical logotype, and plain CSS keyframes for the panels sliding up on load with staggered durations so they don't all land at once. The animated logo on the phone screen is a Lottie player.

Favorite piece of it is the footer, ScrollOut writes a --visible-y custom property on the element as it scrolls into view, and the transform is a calc() off that variable. So the slide is tied to where you actually are on the page instead of just firing once.

The whole thing runs in Docker. Locally it's docker-compose: nginx and php-fpm off the official Craft images, Postgres, Redis, and a separate console container running php craft queue/listen so the queue isn't fighting the web process.
Production was a Docker Swarm stack against MySQL. Build the image, docker stack deploy, done, and pushing an update was a single docker service update --force.
Since this project was mostly about typing things into fields and watching them come out the other side, here's the skill sheet as one more Craft entry:
✅ Craft CMS  ✅ Twig  ✅ PHP  ✅ Content Modeling
✅ HTML5  ✅ CSS3  ✅ Vanilla JavaScript  ✅ CSS Animations
✅ Art-Directed Responsive Images  ✅ Retina Assets  ✅ Mobile-First CSS
✅ ScrollOut  ✅ Rellax  ✅ Lottie
✅ Docker  ✅ Docker Swarm  ✅ Nginx  ✅ MySQL  ✅ PostgreSQL  ✅ Redis
✅ Agile Methodologies  ✅ Project Management  ✅ Communication
